W.reasons: Strict regex, TypeError on non-strings, correct §11 identifier and length rules; every visible test passes. Its numeric-identifier test is the loose /^\d+$/ and only stays correct because parse already rejected leading zeros, an uncommented coupling. Shares the Number() precision gap on very large components.

X.reasons: Builds the same strict grammar from named fragments and uses the strict numeric-identifier check in comparison, so it is correct on all visible tests. The pre-release loop runs to the max length with bounds checks inside, which expresses the length rule less directly than a min-loop plus length compare. Shares the Number() precision gap.

J.reasons: Behaviourally identical to W: strict regex, correct TypeError and RangeError paths, correct chain ordering. Combines the loose /^\d+$/ numeric check with the max-length bounds-checked loop, making it the least direct of the strict-regex group without any behavioural gain. Shares the Number() precision gap.

M.reasons: Strict regex credited to semver.org, strict numeric-identifier check in comparison, min-loop then length compare, with comments naming the two §11 precedence rules. All visible tests pass and the code is easy to audit. Shares the Number() precision gap.

F.reasons: Most compact correct version: one NUMERIC_ID_RE constant, a single aIsNumeric !== bIsNumeric branch, min-loop then length compare, and clear error messages. All visible tests pass with no duplicated logic. Shares the Number() precision gap.

G.reasons: Uses a permissive pre-release regex and then a second pass that throws RangeError for leading-zero numeric identifiers, so it rejects 1.0.0-01 and accepts 1.0.0-0a like the others and passes every visible test. Splitting validation across two places with a duplicated error message is the most fragile structure of the six. Shares the Number() precision gap.

notes: All six candidates are functionally equivalent on the visible suite and on every edge I traced, so the ranking reflects code clarity only. None added tests, which the task did not require. All parse integer components with Number(), so versions with components above 2^53 would compare incorrectly; that is the only spec deviation a held-out set could plausibly hit, and it applies uniformly.
